endorsements.quote: A model should first run in a silent or “shadow” mode in which its outputs are recorded but not acted upon, enabling prospective analyses; progression to operational use should be contingent on pre-specified performance (calibration, sensitivity and false-alarm burden; Table 2 ) being demonstrated in the target population and environment.

Accordingly, we recommend that any operational deployment (i) pre-registers the target label and alarm thresholds, (ii) reports calibration and false-alarm burden alongside accuracy, (iii) requires prospective field validation against a clinically or operationally meaningful outcome, and (iv) retains a human decision-maker in the loop for any withdrawal or medical action.

Once deployed, models require continuous monitoring for data drift and periodic recalibration, transparent documentation of inputs and failure modes, fail-safe default behaviour when signals are missing or out of range, and an auditable human-in-the-loop process for any withdrawal or medical action ( Figure 2 ).
Crucially, trust should rest on independent, external validation rather than on internal development metrics, and each recommendation should be accompanied by an explicit statement of uncertainty.
However, these applications require different evidence thresholds.

defining clear governance roles (data ownership, access, escalation pathways), embedding monitoring within existing medical and performance workflows rather than alongside them, and agreeing in advance how alerts translate into decisions.

unlisted_practices: Retain a human decision-maker in the loop for any withdrawal or medical action based on AI output.
Restrict sensing systems that fail decision-specific agreement thresholds to screening or trend monitoring rather than individual withdrawal decisions.
Anchor validation of sensing systems to a named high-stakes decision using hierarchical, multi-level validation (analytical, criterion, reliability, ecological, decision).
Use uncertainty-aware (probabilistic or Bayesian) models where recommendations can trigger high-stakes actions.
Define explicit labelling rules for AI risk targets and handle missing or delayed signals during algorithm development.
Define who owns sensor data, who can access it, retention period, secondary use, and how informed consent is obtained.
Make participation in physiological monitoring genuinely voluntary with transparent data-use terms.
Apply purpose limitation, data minimisation, athlete access rights, and separation of performance, medical and commercial uses of monitoring data.
Adopt open data formats and interoperability standards for sensor ecosystems.
Involve end-users in system design and train staff in the meaning and limits of each metric.
Provide interpretable outputs with explicit uncertainty and model explainability appropriate to the decision.
Design sensor systems for sport-specific regulatory compatibility, such as unobtrusive form factors or delayed-feedback modes.
Require outcome-specific, context-specific and population-specific validation of wearable device claims.

screen.reason: This is a perspective/framework paper presenting validation and governance recommendations for real-time sensor-based monitoring and AI-driven decision support in human health and performance.
